''non'' Adans.: [[Lophanthus|preoccupied]] }} [[Image:Agastache rupestris2 lg.jpg|thumb|''[[Agastache rupestris]]'' in bloom.]] '''''Agastache''''' ({{IPAc-en|,|æ|g|ə|'|s|t|ɑː|k|iː|}}) is a [[genus]] of aromatic flowering [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial]] plants in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Lamiaceae]]. It contains 22 species, mainly [[native plant|native]] to [[North America]], one species native to eastern [[Asia]]. The common names of the species are a variety of fairly ambiguous and confusing "[[hyssop]]s" and "[[Mentha|mints]]"; as a whole the genus is known as '''giant hyssops''' or '''hummingbird mints'''.{{cite web |url=http://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=4441 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221016235245/https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=4441 |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 16, 2022 |title=''Agastache'' |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] (WCSP) |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] }}{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|page=1136}}{{eFloras|2|100780|Agastache rugosa |first1=Xi-wen |last1=Li |first2=Ian C. |last2=Hedge |volume=17}}{{cite web |url=http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/floranam.php?genere=agastache |title=Genus: ''Agastache'' |website=Altervista Flora of North America}} == Description == Most species are very upright, {{Convert|0.5–3|m|ft|frac=2}} tall, with stiff, angular stems clothed in toothed-edged, lance-shaped leaves ranging from {{Convert|1–15|cm|frac=4}} long and 0.5–11 cm broad depending on the species. Upright spikes of tubular, two-lipped flowers develop at the stem tips in summer. The flowers are usually white, pink, mauve, or purple, with the bracts that back the flowers being of the same or a slightly contrasting color. ==Taxonomy== ''Agastache'' derives from the [[Ancient Greek]] words {{lang|grc|ἄγαν}} ({{grc-tr|ἄγαν}}) "very much" and {{wikt-lang|grc|στάχυς}} ({{grc-tr|στάχυς}}) "ear of grain",{{LSJ|a)/gan|ἄγαν}} and {{LSJ|sta/xus|στάχυς|ref}} describing the flower spikes.{{NPIN |AGFO |access-date=2018-08-08}} The genus was established in 1762 by [[Jan Frederik Gronovius]] in the second edition of his controversial ''Flora Virginica'', based on the specimens and notes of [[John Clayton (botanist)|John Clayton]]. It is a member of subfamily [[Nepetoideae]], which contains a large proportion of the world's aromatic culinary [[herbs]]. Within its subfamily, it belongs to the [[Mentha|mint]] tribe ([[Mentheae]]), and therein to the [[Nepeta|catmint]] [[subtribe]]Formerly treated as tribe [[Nepeteae]]: Sanders (1987). ([[Nepetinae]]). The Nepetinae are robustly supported by [[cladistic]] analyses of [[Morphology (biology)|morphological]] and [[DNA sequence]] data, and were recognized as early as the mid-late 19th century.{{cite journal|last=Sanders|first=Roger W.|year=1987|title=Taxonomy of ''Agastache'' Section ''Brittonastrum'' (Lamiaceae-Nepeteae)|journal=[[Systematic Botany Monographs|Syst. Bot. ''Agastache'']] The closest living relatives of ''Agastache'' are believed to be two very different lineages: One is a group of mostly Asian and usually strongly aromatic and rather robust plants, which contains the typical [[dragonhead]]s (''Dracocephalum''), true hyssops (''[[Hyssopus (plant)|Hyssopus]]''), West Asian dragonheads (''[[Lallemantia]]''), and Japanese catnip (''[[Schizonepeta]]''). By contrast, the other lineage unites the largely scentless and low-growing genera ''[[Glechoma]]'' and ''[[Meehania]]'' which occur widely across the [[Holarctic]]. These three lineages form a tight-knit [[evolutionary radiation|radiation]]; as of 2016, it is not resolved with certainty which of the other two lineages is the [[sister taxon]] of ''Agastache'', but most data place the aromatic group slightly closer. The genus ''Agastache'' seems to have originated as a North American/trans-Beringian offshoot of its radiation about 25 million years ago, in the [[Late Oligocene]].{{cite journal|last1=Drew|first1=Bryan T.|last2=Sytsma|first2=Kennet J.|year=2012|title=Phylogenetics, biogeography, and staminal evolution in the tribe Mentheae (Lamiaceae)|journal=[[American Journal of Botany|Am. J. Bot.]]|volume=99|issue=5|pages=933–953|doi=10.3732/ajb.1100549|pmid=22539517|url=http://www.botany.wisc.edu/sytsma/pdf/DrewSytsma2012.pdf|access-date=2020-07-01|archive-date=2013-01-07|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20130107223055/http://www.botany.wisc.edu/sytsma/pdf/DrewSytsma2012.pdf|url-status=bot: unknown}}{{cite journal|last=Deng|first=Tao|display-authors=etal|year=2015|title=Does the Arcto-Tertiary Biogeographic Hypothesis Explain the Disjunct Distribution of Northern Hemisphere Herbaceous Plants? The Case of ''Meehania'' (Lamiaceae)|journal=[[PLOS ONE]]|volume=10|issue=2|article-number=e0117171|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0117171|pmid=25658699 |pmc=4319762 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1017171D |doi-access=free }} (Fulltext) The sister group of this clade is the core of the Nepetinae, the more or less robust and typically aromatic catmints (''[[Nepeta]]'') and their close relatives''[[Drepanocaryum]]'', ''[[Hymenocrater]]'', ''[[Lophanthus]]'', ''[[Marmoritis]]'': {{harvnb|Drew|Sytsma|2012}} which occur mainly in and around western Asia. The [[monotypic]] and highly distinct ''[[Cedronella]]'' (Canary balm) of [[Macaronesia]] is slightly more distant and seems to be a [[basal (evolution)|basal]] [[relict (biology)|relict]] within the subtribe. Thus, the [[last common ancestor]] of ''Agastache'' and its closest relatives probably was an aromatic Eastern Asian [[perennial]] or [[subshrub]] with [[verticillaster]]s of bluish-purple flowers – i.e. generally very similar to the present-day ''Agastache'' already. The [[plesiomorphic]] appearance of ''Agastache'' is underscored by the fact that some of its species were formerly placed in ''[[Lophanthus]]'' and even ''Cedronella''; essentially, the genus as recognized today was distributed piecemeal across the entire Nepetinae. In general, the evolutionary pattern of the subtribe is a mostly eastward expansion from an origin in the southern or the eastern [[Mediterranean region]], which spread across much of the [[Old World]] and with three genera reached North America. ''Agastache'' is divided into two [[section (botany)|section]]s, sect. ''Agastache'' and sect. ''Brittonastrum''. The former occurs in and around western to central North America, extending across the [[Bering Strait]] into [[East Asia]]. It is characterized by the upper lip of the [[corolla (botany)|corolla]] being small, causing the stalks of the [[stamen|stamina]] to protrude widely. Furthermore, two of the four stamina have curving stalks, which cross those of the other pair. Section ''Brittonastrum'' is found in and around southwestern North America, with the highest diversity in the uplands of northern Mexico. Its members have a more well-developed upper corolla lip, under which the stamina run parallel to each other without crossing, and are entirely hidden from view or only protrude with the anthers and stalk tips. ===Species=== The sections with their species are: ;''Agastache'' sect. Arizona, New Mexico, Chihuahua, Sonora ==Ecology== They grow easily in moist, well-drained soil and prefer a sunny position. Winter hardiness varies; the hardiest is ''[[Agastache foeniculum|A. foeniculum]]'', hardy to [[USDA plant hardiness zone]] 1 in the north of its range; ''[[Agastache nepetoides|A. nepetoides]]'', ''[[Agastache rugosa|A. rugosa]]'', ''[[Agastache scrophulariifolia|A. scrophulariifolia]]'' and ''[[Agastache urticifolia|A. urticifolia]]'' are hardy to zones 3–5 in the northern parts of their ranges. == Cultivation and uses == Propagate from seed or cuttings. Popular cultivars include ''[[Agastache cana|A. cana]]'' 'Heather Queen'. The cultivar 'Blue Fortune'{{cite web|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/109004/Agastache-Blue-Fortune/Details |title=RHS Plant Selector Agastache 'Blue Fortune' AGM / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |date= |access-date=12 March 2020}} has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]. Leaf tips can be eaten and made into teas. ''[[Agastache rugosa]]'' has a history of use in [[Chinese herbology]], where it is called ''huoxiang'' ({{lang-zh|s=藿香|p=huòxiāng}}). ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category}} *{{Missouri Plants |color=White |leaf=opp |genus=Agastache |species=nepetoides |link=1}} *[http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Agastache+foeniculum Plants for a Future] {{Taxonbar|from=Q2020837}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Agastache| ]] [[Category:Lamiaceae genera]]
